## **Fate and Exposure Assessment of Pb Leachate from Hypothetical Breakage Events of Perovskite Photovoltaic Modules**

Sherif A. Khalifa, Sabrina Spatari, Aaron T. Fafarman, Vasilis M. Fthenakis, Patrick L. Gurian, Mira S. Olson, and Jason B. Baxter*

**Cite This:** _Environ. Sci. Technol._ 2023, 57, 5190−5202

**Read Online**

ABSTRACT: Emerging lead halide perovskite (LHP) photovoltaics are undergoing intense research and development due to their outstanding efficiency and potential for low manufacturing costs that render them competitive with existing photovoltaic (PV) technologies. While today’s efforts are focused on stability and scalability of LHPs, the toxicity of lead (Pb) remains a major challenge to their large-scale commercialization. Here, we present a screening-level, EPA-compliant model of fate and transport of Pb leachate in groundwater, soil, and air, following hypothetical catastrophic breakage of LHP PV modules in conceptual utility-scale sites. We estimated exposure point concentrations of Pb in each medium and found that most of the Pb is sequestered in soil. Exposure point concentrations of Pb from the perovskite film fell well below EPA maximum permissible limits in groundwater and air even upon catastrophic release from PV modules at large scales. Background Pb levels in soil can influence soil regulatory compliance, but the highest observed concentrations of perovskite-derived Pb would not exceed EPA limits under our assumptions. Nonetheless, regulatory limits are not definitive thresholds of safety, and the potential for increased bioavailability of perovskite-derived Pb may warrant additional toxicity assessment to further characterize public health risks.

KEYWORDS: _solar cells, regulatory compliance, fate and exposure, lead, toxicity, Monte Carlo_

## **1. INTRODUCTION**

Meeting the world’s climate pledges and electric grid decarbonization goals in the next few decades requires rapid acceleration of solar photovoltaics (PV) deployment as a source of clean and sustainable electricity. Cumulative global PV deployment needs to grow by 10-fold in the next 2 decades from today’s 1 TW to avoid the worst impacts of climate change.[1][,][2] Commercial PV technologies, primarily silicon and CdTe, already supply over 3% of the world’s electricity generation and are the cheapest source of electricity in many parts of the world.[3]

Lead halide perovskites (LHPs) have emerged as an enormously promising lab-scale thin-film PV technology and recently reached record efficiencies of 25.4% for a singlejunction cell and over 29% for a silicon−LHP tandem cell.[4][,][5] Such high efficiencies, combined with their compatibility with high-throughput deposition techniques, projected low capital cost and lower energy payback times and life cycle environmental impacts than state-of-the-art PV technologies demonstrate the enormous potential of LHP PV to develop into a competitive PV module technology to expedite the green energy transition.[6][,][7] The U.S. Department of Energy’s Solar Energy Technology Office (SETO) identified critical barriers and technoeconomic challenges to LHP PV commercialization.[8] Primary directions include improving operational

lifetime to at least 20 years (durability), preserving lab-scale efficiency in industry-relevant cell and module architectures (scalability and manufacturing), and de-risking the potential environmental and human health impacts, particularly of toxic Pb, to meet environmental, health, and safety (EHS) requirements. All are necessary factors to gain consumer confidence and secure investor financing.

Earlier environmental life cycle analysis (LCA) studies revealed the tradeoffs of Pb usage in perovskite PV modules. Our team reported that the life cycle toxicity potential of electricity from LHP PVs over a 20-year operational lifetime would be about 20 times lower than that of current U.S. electricity grid mixes, a reflection of the heavy metal content of the coal employed by some U.S. generation facilities.[9] It would take only about two years of LHP PV electricity generation displacing the grid mix to pay back the total release of Pb in LHP PVs to the environment in a hypothetical (and unlikely) accident event. This amount of Pb is miniscule compared to Pb used in lead-acid ∼ batteries ( 1,000,000 tons of Pb/year), electronic solders, and Pb emissions from state-of-the-art coal power plants.[13] The existing system-level environmental life cycle impact assessments predominantly report both the minimal contribution of Pb to overall perovskite PV system toxicity and the consequential benefits of displacing Pb in existing life cycles of energy systems.

Despite the low Pb content in LHP modules, LHP thin films are reported to be unstable and have been shown to quickly degrade into its cationic precursor (e.g., MAI, FAI) and Pb halide salt, typically PbI2, when exposed to moisture or open air.[14] These Pb salts have appreciable solubility in water, with their _K_ sp on the order of 10[−][9] , making them about 20 orders of magnitude more soluble than Cd in CdTe or Pb in solders of silicon modules.[15][−][17] Some Pb[2+] could react to form PbO and Pb(OH)2 that have even higher solubility, with _K_ sp on the order of 10[−][6] .[18] This higher solubility of Pb in LHP could lead to potentially hazardous soil and groundwater contamination if installed perovskite modules break, for example in an extreme weather event, followed by the release of embodied soluble Pb.[19]

Perovskite-derived Pb has also been reported to be more readily bioavailable for uptake by plant roots and thus could pose a threat of entering the food chain.[20] The increased bioavailability of Pb in LHP is attributed to the presence of the organic cation, which could further decompose into its constituent organic compound and an acid (e.g., MAI ⇌ CH3NH2 + HI). The acid can decrease soil pH and in turn increase the mobility of Pb ions in soil.[21]

The aforementioned perovskite-derived Pb solubility raises important concerns about its potential leachability in various environmental exposure media (i.e., soil, air, water aquifers). A holistic assessment of immediate health risks of LHP PVs to local communities is still needed to quantify the magnitude of risk in different exposure media. Hailegnaw et al. attempted to calculate Pb concentration in soil after breakage of 1 m[2] of LHP module having a 300 nm thick MAPbI3 layer, yielding about 0.42 g of Pb, assuming full release of Pb by a rain event and subsequent infiltration into a similar soil area below the LHP module.[22] The study found that the Pb concentration in soil only increases by 70 mg/kg in the first centimeter of soil, and thus, the Pb concentration from LHP did not result in exceeding typical pre-existing Pb levels in soil. It is unknown whether these conclusions hold in large-scale breakage events, and what the potential risks are in other exposure media like groundwater or air, relevant to commercialization scenarios of LHP PVs. Moody et al. found that, although the actual Pb content in modules is low, substrate choice (i.e., glass vs flexible substrate) could result in a wide range of Pb leachate concentrations in the environment, with subsequent impacts on regulatory compliance.[23] In a recent account, Schmidt et al. found that perovskite-derived Pb is rapidly removed from the aqueous phase and immobilized in the natural soil matrix in only a few hours.[24] While that experimental sequential soil

extraction showed promise for lead sequestration, it used only one type of loamy sand and a chloride-enriched simulated rainwater composition profile with neutral pH, which is different from the conventional simulated weakly acidic rainwater used in standardized leaching tests (e.g., SPLP by U.S. EPA).

There is still scarcity in both experimental and modeling literature attempting to identify and understand the industryscale factors that could affect human exposure and associated health risks from LHP-derived Pb, particularly the fate of Pb in exposure media under different environmental conditions.[25] Potential Pb toxicity hazards for human health depend primarily on the exposure concentrations of Pb compounds in exposure media as well as the type and severity of exposure response of the human body to the Pb form in the exposure media. Prior work of Babayigit et al. summarized the kinetics of Pb intoxication on various human organs, while also highlighting the need to estimate potential exposure point concentrations that may be available for human intake in different media upon module breakage.[26] The International Energy Agency Photovoltaic Power System Programme (IEA PVPS) published on human health risk assessment modeling methods for screening the magnitude of risk of heavy metal contaminants of commercial PV technologies (Pb in silicon and Cd in CdTe) after breakage events.[27] The report follows a conservative, screening-level approach to quantify the magnitude of exposure point concentrations and evaluate whether a more in-depth risk analysis is warranted. The IEA PVPS report also claims that methods therein could apply to evaluating risks of emerging technologies like perovskite PVs.

In view of these considerations and to quantify an order-ofmagnitude estimation for Pb exposure risks of LHP PVs in near-commercial scenarios, here we report a screening-level assessment of human exposure potential to Pb from perovskite PV examined for conceptual industry-scale scenarios with onsite breakage events followed by subsequent leaching of embodied Pb by rain and transport into the surrounding environment. The objective of this work is to estimate potential Pb exposure point concentrations in soil, potable groundwater aquifers, and air after a breakage event in rainy conditions of utility-scale LHP modules using an EPAcompliant fate and transport modeling approach. Then, we compare Pb point concentrations in exposure media against regulatory maximum permissible limits (MPLs) and identify sensitive factors and parameters that may warrant a more detailed risk assessment. We report soil screening Pb concentrations by applying a soil−soil pore water compartment modeling approach for PV risk assessment that could overcome mass conservation violations inherent in conventional infinite source fate and transport modeling approaches.

This study provides insight into immediate human exposure risks associated with the accidental release of Pb from prospective utility-scale perovskite PV installations. We note that having exposure point concentrations below regulatory limits is an important first step but is not a sufficient condition to ensure public safety. Some literature suggests that there is no safe exposure level for Pb, especially for young children.[28][,][29] Increased bioavailability of perovskite-derived Pb may indicate that generic Pb MPLs may not be sufficiently restrictive.[20] Therefore, this work is not a full guide, nor should it be interpreted as conclusive evidence for human health risks associated with LHP PV deployment. This study can also be viewed as an ongoing effort to select appropriate screening-

level methods to model health risks of leachable contaminants in PV modules.

## **2. METHODS AND MODELING APPROACH**

This study followed an exposure risk assessment framework, as developed by the U.S. EPA, U.S. National Academy of Sciences, and the International Organization for Standardization, ISO 31010, for risk assessment techniques.[30][−][32] This framework included the identification of concerning chemical contaminants (hazard identification), environmental fate and transport modeling to estimate Pb exposure dose in exposure media (exposure assessment), comparison of calculated exposure doses to health screening values (dose− response assessment), and quantification of robustness of results to parameter uncertainties using Monte Carlo simulations (risk characterization).

PV-specific screening-level human health risk assessment methods are outlined in the IEA PVPS T12-15:2019 report, which itself builds on the methods outlined in the International Electrotechnical Commission Technical Specification report, IEC TS 62994.[27][,][33] Our study follows the screening methods outlined in those reports and expands upon them to address limiting assumptions related to Pb leachability in perovskite PV modules. Particularly, we revisit the limitations of models that are based on an infinite source of heavy metal contaminants.

**2.1. Scenarios Examined and Conceptual Site Model.** We assessed human health risks of Pb exposure from hypothetical breakage of emerging perovskite-on-silicon tandem modules in two conceptual utility-scale PV sites of size 100 MWp and 500 MWp under typical low rate and complete (i.e., catastrophic) breakage scenarios. The choice of 100 MWp reflects today’s average installed plant capacity,[34] while a choice of 500 MWp reflects recent trends in increased site capacities to meet decarbonization goals.[35] We chose perovskite-on-silicon tandem technology due to its near-term commercialization prospects, but results and conclusions would not be significantly different for single-junction perovskite or all-perovskite tandem configurations. Based on perovskite-on-silicon technology, we assumed an average module efficiency of 24% as a reasonable market entry target to calculate the site area in each scenario. We obtained this module efficiency by assuming ∼6% loss compared to the current record efficiency of 29.8% for a perovskite-on-tandem cell.[5] Pb content is calculated based on high-performing Cs0.25FA0.75PbI3 perovskite structure assuming 1 _μ_ m (micron) film thickness. Our “typical breakage” scenarios assume a breakage rate of 0.04% of site modules based on the current warranty returns of analogous CdTe thin-film technology.[27] While there is currently no record of fielded perovskite module durability, perovskite modules will need to pass extended reliability testing and other imposed quality control and safety testing prior to their market entry. Full breakage scenarios represent an improbable site-wide decimation after a natural (i.e., tornado, hurricane) or anthropogenic disaster. Such events have seldom been reported. The PV industry is vigilant to the occurrence of natural disasters that might increase in frequency and intensity as climate change worsens and PV deployment potentially expands into disaster-prone locations. PV design for stability and durability that can withstand the harshest outdoor conditions continues to be a quickly evolving area in perovskite and silicon PV research.[36][−][38]

**2.2. Pb Release Mechanism, Exposure Route, and Population.** In this study, the hypothetical release of Pb is modeled to occur through leaching of the Pb heavy metal to rainwater that falls on broken perovskite modules after a catastrophic failure event. Pb is transported in rainwater runoff to site soil and infiltrates into a nearby groundwater aquifer that is assumed to be a drinking source, and Pb is also mobilized from soil to air by dust emissions. Figure 1 shows a schematic of the three exposure pathways examined, along with our screening-level approach to estimate potential Pb exposure concentrations. Worst-case assumptions were made at every decision point in each transport pathway, even if the actual chances of an extreme situation happening are miniscule. This exercise reinforces our screening-level, conservative approach to exposure estimation.

The exposure population is modeled to be onsite workers or offsite residents, who may be exposed to impacted soils through dermal contact or incidental ingestion, drinking from public water supplies that use potentially contaminated groundwater aquifer as a water supply, or inhaling Pbcontaminated air.

Exposure point concentrations are calculated under the unlikely assumption that full Pb release occurs instantaneously upon breakage and that broken perovskite modules go unmitigated for an exposure period of 1 year. These assumptions are very conservative because site owners/ contractors routinely monitor their system for faulty modules and would be expected to carry out site contamination testing and remediation protocols following a large-scale breakage event. Nonetheless, we chose to model this limiting case as a health-protective approach.

**2.3. Pb Leachate Concentration.** The amount of Pb released upon module damage is the most influential input parameter for calculating exposure concentrations via fate and transport modeling. In this study, Pb leachate concentrations in rainwater runoff are taken as the U.S. EPA Method 1312 Synthetic Precipitation Leaching Procedure (SPLP) test result of perovskite modules in the literature.[39] The SPLP testing procedure includes full submersion of broken modules of ∼1 − cm size in weakly acidic leaching solution (pH = 4.0 5.0) in a liquid/solid ratio of 20:1 for a total duration of 18 h. These conditions are not tailored for PV site environments. Development of PV-relevant toxicity assessment is an area that still needs to be addressed for more accurate PV risk assessment.

Figure 1. Conceptual site model for evaluating potential Pb leachate release from perovskite PV modules. Pb exposure point concentrations in soil, groundwater, and air were evaluated using tailored screening-level approaches.

To date, there are only two literature articles that report leaching test results for perovskite cells.[40][,][41] Both articles relied on their lab-scale perovskite cell architectures to conduct their tests. Commercial perovskite modules are likely to have fewer manufacturing defects, enhanced durability, and possibly entirely different architectures with commercially relevant materials, deposition, and encapsulation choices compared to their lab-scale counterparts. More rugged encapsulation and lamination in commercial modules would likely act as a strong barrier between rainwater and embodied Pb in the absorber film.

Panthi et al. reported that the U.S. EPA toxicity characterization leaching potential (TCLP) results used for hazardous waste classification for a pristine (i.e., unbroken) perovskite minimodule with a 300 nm film encapsulated between two 2 mm thick pieces of glass had a Pb leachate concentration of 0.959 mg/L.[40] Using thicker encapsulation between 5 mm glass sheets reduced Pb leachate to 0.315 mg/L, but this thickness is much larger than what is practical for fielded PV modules. A non-encapsulated device yielded the maximum Pb leachate of 4.18 mg/L, which was still lower than the 5.0 mg/L threshold for hazardous waste classification according to the Resource Recovery and Conservation Act (RCRA) guidelines. TCLP results will depend sensitively on the thickness of the perovskite layer and the choices for module lamination and encapsulation.

Su et al. reported the SPLP test result of 5.5 mg/L for Pb leachate of a broken unencapsulated, laboratory-fabricated perovskite cell.[41] The Pb leachate in a second SPLP cycle was reduced to 0.282 mg/L, indicating that almost all Pb was washed out from a broken module upon first contact with water. For single-point exposure estimates, we used the SPLP result of 5.5 mg/L as the Pb leachate concentration from perovskite modules. However, this concentration should be viewed as an upper limit because of the lack of lamination and encapsulation of the cell measured with the SPLP,[41] and our reported exposure calculations are also likely higher than what would be expected if industry-standard modules had been tested. We call out the need for TCLP and SPLP results from commercially relevant module constructions and realistic conditions.

**2.4. Fate and Transport Modeling.** In exposure assessment, screening-level fate and transport mathematical models are used to estimate exposure point concentrations of Pb in soil, groundwater, and air media given Pb concentration in the impacted medium, modeled here to be Pb-contaminated

rainwater runoff. We used the total amount of embodied Pb released to carry out the calculations for exposure point concentrations in three independent Pb pathways: transport to site soil via rainwater infiltration, transport from vadose (i.e., unsaturated subroot) zone soil pore water to potable groundwater aquifer, and transport from soil to ambient air via dust emissions. Similar pathways were modeled for Pb in c- Si and Cd in CdTe in the IEA PVPS report.[27] We started by applying similar mathematical models to the perovskite PV case, and then we compared the results to a compartment modeling approach in an attempt to invoke mass conservation of Pb in the exposure media. The following two subsections outline the modeling methods applied to estimate Pb exposure point concentrations.

_2.4.1. _2.4.2. Groundwater._ The migration of Pb through the soil column to a potable aquifer underneath reduces the leachate concentration by attenuation processes including adsorption in the vadose zone and further dilution and attenuation in the saturated water table zone. While we chose to focus only on breakage-related air exposure risks in utility-scale systems, fire events could accompany breakage events, especially in rooftop systems on wood-frame houses. Fire events may release Pb into the air, but we did not assess such scenarios due to the lack of experimental data quantifying the extent of release. We note that the potential Pb emissions during fires may vary depending on the module encapsulation. For example, experimental investigations by Fthenakis et al. showed that double-glass-encapsulated CdTe module would sequester most of the Cd during residential fires, whereas without adequate encapsulation, Cd would be emitted into the air.[46] An investigation of perovskite fire risks by Conings et al. that combined lab-scale experiments and atmospheric dispersion − modeling concurred with the significant benefits of glass glass encapsulation for containing Pb during fires. The study reported that Pb concentrations in air downwind from a 5 kW residential PV installation engulfed in a fire would be many times below U.S. regulatory air quality standards.[47] The study also concluded that Pb risks were significantly higher without glass encapsulation. Potential emissions due to fires in largescale PV systems have not been evaluated.

## **3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION**

## **3.1. Exposure Assessment and Risk Characterization.**

_3.1.1. Soil._ Dissolving all Pb in the modules at the SPLP concentration, resulting in _C_ leachate of 5.5 mg/L, would require 0.25 m of rainfall over the module area. Runoff into soil with a porosity of 0.3 would result in a stratified soil depth of 0.8 m. It would take several months of average rainfall to accumulate 0.25 m of precipitation in many parts of the world. However, 0.25 m of rainfall is possible during a single hurricane event that may also have sufficient wind speeds to catastrophically damage the modules.

If released lead were distributed uniformly through the stratified depth of 0.8 m, our calculations show that the rise in single-point concentration of Pb in subsurface soil would be 1.1 mg/kg. Conversely, if all of the Pb were confined to the top soil, defined here as the first cm, the released Pb would have a

concentration of 91 mg/kg. This scenario could result from a series of lighter rainfall events following module breakage. There are currently no U.S. laws specifically regulating Pb emissions for perovskite PVs or other PV systems. More broadly, the U.S. EPA maximum permissible limits (MPLs) for Pb in soil are 1200 and 400 mg/kg for nonplay and play zones, respectively.[48] These limits trigger qualification for federal funding for soil cleanup and remediation purposes; however, concentrations below this threshold do not guarantee or imply that they are safe. Regulatory compliance of accidental perovskite module breakage also depends on the pre-existing background Pb levels in the soil. Pre-existing Pb levels can vary significantly, typically between 70−600 mg/kg but sometimes already exceeding 1200 mg/kg, depending on the local history of industrial activities in the region and on the soil type.[49] Accidental release of Pb into soil with high background levels exceeding >300 mg/kg could pose an increased risk of exceeding residential play-zone soil limits.

Utility-scale solar arrays are not likely to be near play zones, but degraded land with higher levels of contamination may be used as sites for future solar farms. In that case, the background Pb levels should be measured at the time of site selection to ensure ample margin with respect to the 1200 mg/kg limit. We note again that our methods do not apply for residential rooftop solar arrays where released Pb could be concentrated at the downspout, the outlet of which could be in a potential play zone.

As discussed in Section 2.1, Pb-specific _K_ d values depend on a range of parameters, including soil types (e.g., loamy, sand, clay), soil pH, and speciation of Pb ions in the aqueous phase. For example, Pb may precipitate out of solution into an insoluble salt phase if soluble concentrations exceed 4 mg/L at pH = 4 and about 0.2 mg/L at pH = 8.[21] These solubility limits can be many times lower in the presence of chloride or phosphate ions. At the studied SPLP concentration of 5.5 mg/ L and its corresponding weak acidic conditions, the calculated Pb soil concentration could therefore represent a salt precipitation phenomenon rather than inclusion into soil particles. The solubility limits also play a role in the volume of water needed to leach embodied Pb from modules.

To examine the robustness of our results, we conducted a Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis to study the effect of _K_ d values and _C_ leachate concentrations on Pb levels in subsurface soil. Both parameters were varied using a triangular distribution. Lower and upper bounds of _K_ d values were selected to represent different soil types (sandy loamy, claylike, sandy peat) and extreme soil pH (pH = 4.5−9.0) from EPA and Swedish Nuclear Fuel and Waste Management (SKB) reports.[50][,][51] _K_ d values of 20 and 44,000 L/kg were selected in this study, with a likely value of 900 L/kg. Lower and upper bounds of _C_ leachate were selected to represent maximum and minimum volumes of rainwater necessary to wash off Pb from LHP modules; values selected are 1.0 and 440 mg/L (the solubility of the PbI2 precursor) as the lower and upper limits, respectively, with likely value of 5.5 mg/L from the available SPLP test result. Lower and upper bounds of _K_ d values represent extremely porous and impermeable soil types, respectively, along with acidic and basic soil environments. A _K_ d value of 20 L/kg, as might be found in moisturerich deep peat soil in a weakly acidic environment conducive to ionized Pb[2+] , represents the highest risk to groundwater contamination. _3.1.2. Groundwater._ Table 2 shows the calculated maximum single-point Pb concentrations in groundwater. Pb levels in all scenarios fall below EPA drinking water limits of 0.015 mg/L. The DAF model incorporates implicit worst-case assumptions that the groundwater extraction well is located 25 ft horizontally from the breakage site and that the contaminant from every broken module is transported to the same groundwater well. These assumptions are overly conservative in the case of large-scale PV sites that can extend over kilometers, and thus, only Pb from a small fraction of the

broken modules might be captured by a nearby unconfined groundwater aquifer site.

In the IEA PVPS report, the vadose zone soil pore water, represented by the SPLP concentration, is directly divided by the DAF factor. This approach could yield a conservative estimation for stable, sparingly soluble Pb forms in solders of c- Si with low SPLP concentrations and low _K_ d. However, the direct representation of Pb concentration in vadose zone soil pore water by the SPLP concentration neglects the impact of attenuation processes during contaminant migration down into the water table and also the partitioning of the contaminant to soil, both of which play an important role in reducing contaminant concentration before the contaminated water reaches an aquifer. It is highly unlikely for the rainwater runoff to penetrate deep into the vadose zone without first infiltrating into the soil column, except in the case of a runoff to surface water body or through open fractures (i.e., macropores), which are outside the scope of this study. Even then, careful consideration should be given to contaminant attenuation chemistry (i.e., biodegradation, chemical degradation) and other aquifer-related factors (i.e., aquifer size, thickness, renewal rates) in addition to dilution modeled by DAFs.

The site-specific risk assessment would evaluate the impact of more subtle conditions (i.e., preferential pathways, infiltration rates) on groundwater contamination risk. Immediate investigation after catastrophic events is prescribed.

**3.2. Considerations of Bioavailability and Current Soil Screening Regulations.** This study has estimated potential exposure point concentrations upon different breakage scenarios for Pb perovskite PVs via a fate and transport modeling approach. We have referred to EPA regulatory limits to provide screening-level context for these concentrations. However, we acknowledge that these regulatory limits are broadly written and may not necessarily include important considerations of bioavailability of different types of Pb. The extrapolation of exact approaches to regulatory frameworks used to determine MPLs may be complex or impossible. There are additional concerns related to perovskite-derived Pb bioavailability and biotoxicity, and whether these factors are more severe for it than for Pb from other sources. Bioavailability is one of many important factors that influence risk assessment for human and ecological toxicity, given a starting point of exposure point concentrations. The absence of a reference dose or daily intake limit for Pb indicates that adverse health effects could result even at very low concentrations.

It is already known that PbI2, a product of perovskite decomposition, has much higher solubility than other forms of Pb from solder or Cd in CdTe or CdS in solar cells. Some studies claim that the uptake and toxicity of Pb from perovskites are more severe than other sources of Pb such as

Pb(NO3)2.[53][,][54] However, others claim that the fate and sequestration of Pb are similar regardless of the source,[52] as is the toxicity.[53] Recent work by Hutter may help reconcile these findings by considering the role of iodide.[54] They report that PbI2, MAPbI3, and MAI induced toxicity response in _Arabidopsis thaliana_ at 1-2 orders of magnitude smaller concentration than Pb(NO3)2 and PbBr2, concluding that iodide plays an important role in the toxicity. They conclude that the levels of lead release from solar module failures would not be significantly toxic but that more focus should be placed on iodide, which may be. For human health risk assessment purposes, bioavailability does not impact exposure point concentrations presented herein. Rather, bioconcentration factors become a critical input to calculating Pb levels in affected organisms (e.g., human blood levels, concentrations in plants, etc).

In this study, exposure concentrations in soil, groundwater, and air are compared to EPA limits on Pb levels in bare soil, which are 400 mg/kg in a play area and 1200 mg/kg in a nonplay area. These thresholds for superfund site soil quality standards are designed to trigger potential mitigation efforts and do not imply that lower levels are universally safe for human and ecological health. Additionally, states could have their own more restrictive limits, such as California, which imposes thresholds of 80 mg/kg for Pb residential soil screening level and 500 mg/kg for commercial/industrial zones.[55] The 80 mg/kg threshold represents the soil concentration for which sensitive groups like children could experience an incremental increase of 1 _μ_ g/dL Pb blood level via ingestion, re-suspension, and dermal contact.

As mentioned in Section 1, perovskite-derived Pb has considerably higher solubility than other common sources of Pb. The increased solubility facilitates Pb[2+] to be readily absorbed in plant or animal tissue. The measure of ease of dose absorbance is referred to as bioavailability. Prior experimental work by Li et al. showed that spiking Pb levels in natural soil by 10% via a Pb perovskite precursor led to a 100% increase in mean Pb concentration in the root zone of planted mint.[20] The authors warned against introducing a safety threshold level of Pb levels in soil because of bioavailability concerns.

On the other hand, Oorts et al. attempted to quantify the role of Pb[2+] bioavailability on ecological soil quality standards and found that soils freshly spiked with Pb[2+] salts similar to those in perovskite PV exhibited higher Pb bioavailability and lower toxic thresholds than long-term aged and leached equivalents.[56] The results of the comparative toxicity tests of the study indicate that Pb soil screening thresholds could be increased by up to a factor of 4 compared to thresholds determined using freshly spiked soils. Identifying the timeseries variation of bioavailability of heavy metals in soils should be combined with the knowledge of total extractable concentrations of metals in media to identify proper remediation efforts (e.g., excavation of top soil).

While there is still some debate on methods, including bioavailability, considerations in soil screening levels are important to make those levels relevant to local field conditions in a first-tier risk assessment. One such way is to use relevant time-series sorption values or desorption measurements to screen bioavailable concentrations in addition to total extractable concentrations in exposure media.[57] Unfortunately, this type of data is not available at the time of this study. For a human risk assessment, the EPA has published its own guidance on assessing the oral bioavailability of Pb in soils for

human health risk assessment purposes.[58] Future human health risk assessment studies should be able to utilize this guidance along with exposure assessment herein to characterize healthbased risks in PV sites to determine if site-specific risk assessment is warranted.

**3.3. Risk Mitigation.** Thus far, we have shown the screening-level Pb single-point and Monte Carlo exposure point concentrations in soil, groundwater, and air and compared them to health-based screening levels mandated by U.S. EPA regulations. We found that under our healthprotective assumptions, Pb levels in all three exposure media fall below EPA regulatory limits when considering only the Pb potentially accidentally released from perovskite PV panels. Additional consideration is warranted if the pre-existing background Pb in media is high due to previous contamination. Now, we discuss potential risk mitigation strategies to control Pb release into the environment in connection to some limitations of this study.

Strategically siting perovskite modules in arid and remote locations far from people, agricultural crops, and aquifers could significantly reduce potential exposure risks. Many utility-scale solar farms are already placed in such areas, for example, in the desert southwest region of the United States. In the unlikely event of breakage, there would be relatively small risk to local ecologies.

Current research in module-level mitigation of the release of perovskite-derived Pb is focused on encapsulation, capture, and recycle (ECR) approaches. Current PV modules are encapsulated with high bond strength polymers (e.g., ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA)) and other mechanical stress-resistant backsheets (e.g., Surlyn) in some module designs. Perovskite modules are likely to have a glass−glass laminated buildup analogous to thin-film CdTe technology, which can also boost their reliability and durability. Alternate encapsulant materials such as epoxy resins have been shown to retain perovskite stability and inhibit moisture and air ingress under hail-like conditions.[59] The strong lamination layer protects modules from breaking open in harsh outdoor weather conditions. It has been shown that the encapsulant layer in current modules is so strong that crushed modules in landfill compactors maintained the front (and back) encapsulant layer. Encapsulation and lamination also limit the exposure of embedded module components to only the crack surface area.[60] Recent experimental innovations also report the addition of prelaminated ultrathin Pb-absorbing tapes that can be attached to both sides of modules and can sequester up to 99.9% of potential Pb release in exposure to moisture.[61][,][62] Other studies also reported the use of self-healing epoxy polymers that can suppress up to 95% of potential Pb leakage.[59][,][63] These modulelevel innovations may provide additional leaching protection and minimize the need for site-specific permitting, which is time-intensive and hinders PV deployment goals, as long as cost competitiveness of the technology is preserved.

Recently, commercial modules started using thicker front glass layers to compensate for self-stress of evolving thinner absorber wafers and films.[64] Thicker front glass further increases the durability of PV modules and lowers their breakage risks. Commercial modules are marked as hail-safe in their product datasheets.

The presence of Pb can also incentivize the implementation of extended producer responsibility (EPR) as was the case for U.S.-based CdTe technology. Under EPR, module manufacturers may have module takeback programs to collect

decommissioned or damaged perovskite modules and safely handle their end-of-life management optimally through materials recycling. Several proof-of-concept perovskite recycling line designs were reported to capture nearly 100% of embodied Pb via solvent extraction.[65][−][68] Technoeconomic and life cycle analysis of such lines are still missing in the literature. Nonetheless, implementing circular economy principles in this early stage of perovskite PV deployment is essential to phase out module waste and ensure closed-loop materials recycling.[69][−][71]

Several site-level mitigation and treatment strategies also exist for the unlikely event of Pb release. Fitting PV sites with stormwater management features (e.g., swales, retention pods) and field amendments such as bentonite clay could prevent Pb leachate from reaching water exposure media such as surface water sources or groundwater wells. Cost-effectiveness, scalability, and remediation efficiencies are a few important factors that should be considered on a site-specific basis.

In the unlikely and unfortunate event of Pb release, several treatment methods of Pb-contaminated soils are recommended by the EPA, including extraction processes (e.g., soil washing) and solidification/precipitation techniques (e.g., alkalization) to immobilize Pb into concrete-like masses followed by cleanups.[72] These methods have been verified by the EPA as commercially viable methods already practiced today.

**3.4. Outcomes and Limitations of This Study, and**

**Future Research Needs.** This study provided a screeninglevel exposure assessment of potential accidental Pb leachate emissions from lead halide perovskite photovoltaic modules in utility-scale solar farms. Methods presented here can be of value to further health exposure and risk assessment of lead halide perovskite photovoltaics and allow researchers to examine contaminant migration in water, soil, and air without developing more complex finite-source mass transfer models. The compartment model attempts to address the appreciably high solubility of perovskite-derived Pb compared to other forms of regulated Pb by assuming equilibrium of the contaminant between soil and soil pore water. This modification improves upon the assumption of an infinite contaminant source reported in previous works on risk assessment for less soluble Pb solders in c-Si. However, experimental, site-specific _K_ d values for perovskite-derived Pb in soils from potential solar farm sites would narrow the uncertainty in the results.

Results show that average Pb exposure point concentrations in both subsurface soil and the top centimeter of soil fall below EPA play-zone limits, as long as pre-existing Pb levels in soil are not abnormally high. Cases that could potentially exceed EPA maximum permissible limits for soil include siting solar arrays on soils that already have high background Pb levels or concentration of contaminated rainwater into areas much smaller than the module area. In light of this uncertainty, rapid investigation of soil, including soil sampling, would be encouraged immediately after a catastrophic breakage event to determine whether the Pb level in soil is high enough to warrant soil cleanup efforts. Comparison of exposure point concentrations calculated herein to EPA limits alone is not enough to draw universal conclusions about perovskite PV environmental health and safety. The conducted exposure assessment needs to be combined with the estimation of Pb intake and toxicity assessment to characterize specific human health risks.

We found that single-point and Monte Carlo maximum Pb concentrations in groundwater in all site sizes and breakage rates fall below EPA regulatory limits. This result is ascribed to the strong binding of Pb to soil upon contact with the contaminated rainwater runoff to the soil. Pb exposure point concentrations in air also fall well below EPA regulatory limits for all four scenarios. Typical (i.e., noncatastrophic) breakage events that we modeled yielded Pb exposure point concentrations in groundwater that are several orders of magnitude below EPA limits. We have not considered the fate of Pb leachate through soil via preferential pathways (e.g., macroscale fissures) that could circumvent contaminant attenuation and pose a greater risk to groundwater contamination.

Higher tandem module efficiencies and smaller perovskite film thicknesses than the conservative inputs modeled here (24% and 1 _μ_ m, respectively) would both result in smaller Pb intensity per MW of PV power generation. These improvements would therefore reduce Pb emissions and the resulting exposure point concentrations if modules were to break.

This study is limited by the absence of Pb leachate concentration data from SPLP testing of commercial-grade perovskite modules. We have used SPLP of an unencapsulated lab-scale cell and TCLP of a lab-scale minimodule as the best approximations.[40][,][41] These substitutes may not reflect the performance and durability anticipated for and required of commercial products. Experimental work is needed to understand the impact of different module architectures and encapsulation materials on potential Pb leaching from broken modules.

A wide selection of risk mitigation strategies is available at the module, site, and system levels. Site selection, soil amendments, and the implementation of Pb-absorbing tapes during the lamination phase of module assembly can all reduce the risk of exceeding EPA limits even in the unlikely event of catastrophic breakage and Pb release. Continued research efforts to address and eliminate different forms of perovskite degradation, most notably moisture-induced degradation, are critical for improved environmental health and safety as well as long-term reliability of perovskite PV modules in the field.

Careful interpretation of this work is emphasized. This work should not be considered as terminal conclusive evidence regarding the potential human health impacts of lead halide perovskite PVs in utility-scale solar farms. Rather, the authors attempted to identify more relevant and accurate exposure assessment methods to lead halide perovskite technology. These methods may extend previous PV risk assessment methods and thus may be used to identify sensitive parameters, analyze toxicity risks of other inorganic or organic species, and provide helpful feedback for safer deployment of perovskite photovoltaics.
